s: The medina's Friday mosque, sacred ground since antiquity
w: The historic Friday mosque at the heart of Tangier's old medina, its present form dating to the early 19th century under the Alaouite sultans. The ground beneath it has carried a succession of religious buildings since antiquity, one structure quietly replacing another for longer than anyone's kept precise count.
_facts: Historic main mosque (Friday mosque) of Tangier, located in the city's old medina
Current design dates from the early 19th century, Alaouite period
Site has been occupied by a succession of religious buildings since antiquity

w: Tangier's only bullring, raised by the Spanish in 1950 with room for over 13,000 spectators. Abandoned for years now, its terraces stand empty where crowds once roared for the corrida; locals still count it among the city's important pieces of historical heritage, even deep into its decline.
_facts: Also known as Plaza de Toros or place des arenes; the only bullring in Tangier
Inaugurated in 1950 by the Spanish, capacity of 13,013 seats
Abandoned for several years; remains an important piece of historical heritage tangerois

s: The 'Church of the Sands' for Tangier's French community
w: Built between 1949 and 1953 to serve Tangier's French community during the years of the International Zone, this parish church carries nearly as many names as parishioners: Notre-Dame-de-l'Assomption, Sainte-Jeanne-d'Arc, or simply Eglise des Sables, the Church of the Sands.
_facts: Formal name: Church of Our Lady of the Assumption and of Saint Joan of Arc
Also known as Sainte-Marie-Sainte-Jeanne-d'Arc or Eglise des Sables ('Sands Church')
Parish church built 1949-1953 for the French community during the Tangier International Zone

s: Former British consulate, now a contemporary art gallery
w: Housed in Tangier's former British consulate near St. Andrew's Church, this gallery opened as the city's Museum of Contemporary Art in 1986. A 2006 redevelopment brought a new name and a 2007 reopening as the Galerie d'Art Contemporain Mohamed Drissi, a diplomatic address turned artistic second act.
_facts: Housed in the building of the former British consulate near the Church of St. Andrew
Opened as the Museum of Contemporary Art in 1986
Redeveloped in 2006, renamed and reopened April 12, 2007 as Galerie d'Art Contemporain Mohamed Drissi

s: 93m hilltop where the Mediterranean meets the Atlantic
w: Rising 93 metres above the city, this hill is one of the few spots in Tangier where the geography that defines the place becomes visible at a glance: the Mediterranean on one side, the Atlantic on the other, the two seas meeting close to where you're standing.
_facts: Hill in Tangier, elevation 93 metres above sea level
Overlooks the city between the Mediterranean and the Atlantic

s: A sultan's unused palace, later Italy's Casa d'Italia
w: Built in 1912-13 as the intended retirement residence of Sultan Abdelhafid after his forced abdication, never actually used for that purpose. Italy bought it in 1927, renamed it Palazzo Littorio, then Casa d'Italia in 1943, running schools and a hospital there. Idle since a renovation in the early 2000s.
_facts: Historic structure at 23 Rue Mohammed Ben Abdelouhab, Hasnouna neighbourhood, Tangier
Built 1912-1913 as intended residence of former Sultan Abdelhafid following his abdication, never used for that purpose
Purchased by Italy in 1927, renamed Palazzo Littorio; hosted schools and a hospital
1943 Badoglio government renamed it Casa d'Italia; renovated in early 2000s; long underutilized
